## From the repo

### Intent
What this repository is for, from its .zbuild/vision.md. It steers every
choice you make.


### zBuild — Vision

> The North Star for zBuild — it steers how zBuild is built. The README distills it; the wiki references it; every pipeline run is steered by it.

#### Intent
zBuild turns a delivery process into data — templates and plugins — so software is built the same disciplined way every time. We build zBuild the way zBuild builds: a minimal core, with all behavior plugin-delivered and template-composed. A good change is small, aligned to the spec, proven by a test, and wired into the live path — never scaffolding that looks finished but does nothing.

#### Principles
- **Target-agnostic by contract** — zBuild builds *any* repository, not itself; the engine and plugins never assume the target's language, layout, or that zBuild is the target. Target knowledge lives in data — templates, config, per-repo overrides — never in code.
- **Spec wins over drift** — KEEPERS, ARCHITECTURE, and the ADRs are the source of truth; when code disagrees, the code changes, not the spec.
- **Small engine, behavior at the edges** — keep the core tiny; add capability as plugins composed in templates, never by growing the engine.
- **Safety is structural** — all model-bound text passes one redaction chokepoint; state is atomic and resumable; scope is governed at every boundary.
- **Models are data, not code** — selection flows through the router and config tiers; never hardcode a model name.
- **Prove behavior, then wire it** — every change ships a test that fails without it and connects to the live path; green-but-inert is a defect.
- **Fail closed, never silent** — gates block on real problems and say why; bounded cycles and recovery drive work to done.
- **Dogfood every change** — build zBuild with zBuild; if the pipeline can't ship it, fix the pipeline.

### Rules
These are this repository's rules (.zbuild/prompts/rules.md). Work that
breaks one is wrong, whoever wrote it.

- Bash only, and match the file you are in: 4-space indent, LF line endings, a final newline, no trailing whitespace (.editorconfig). Everything must pass `shellcheck` with the repo's .shellcheckrc.
- Never pipe anything into `grep -q`, and never pipe into a bare `head`, in any `.sh` file, test files included. The reader exits early, the writer takes SIGPIPE, and under `set -o pipefail` the line fails for a reason nothing logs. Use a here-string instead: `grep -q PATTERN <<< "$var"`, or run grep on the file directly: `grep -q PATTERN "$file"`. `tests/unit/sigpipe-antipattern-guard-test.sh` fails the suite on any violation; a genuinely safe pipe is annotated `# sigpipe-ok: <reason>`.
- Never name a model (haiku, sonnet, opus, …) in code; model selection goes through core/router and config/models.json.
- A test must be able to fail: assert what is required, never what the code happens to do.
- Never edit anything under `legacy-DoNotUse/`.

#### Facts about this repo
- `ZBUILD_*` environment variables are set by the engine at dispatch (the artifact dir, the stage's input index `ZBUILD_STAGE_INPUTS`, the issue, the run). They are trusted engine inputs, not user or attacker input.
- A stage never names another stage's output — not its output name, not its file. The engine hands every stage every earlier stage's latest output, and a stage finds what it needs by what it contains (scripts/lib/earlier-output.sh; ADR-055 §1). A plugin that names another stage's output is a defect.
- Every stage writes a v2 result (`result_contract`, `verdict`, `disposition`, `reason`, detail under `data`) on every exit path, and exits 0 or 1 (ADR-054).
- `[SPEC-n]` / `[#<issue>/SPEC-n]` tags in a test tie an assertion to one issue's acceptance contract. A tag that belongs to another issue must never be changed or removed.

## What you own

You are checking whether a finished CHANGE does what an ISSUE asked for.

One verdict on the whole issue: does the DIFF meet every requirement the issue
states, in full — including what its tests must catch?

Answer with one line for every requirement in ISSUE REQUIREMENTS, by its id:

MET: <id>
UNMET: [fix-code] <id> | WHY: <what the change does not do> | QUOTE: <quote>
UNMET: [fix-design] <id> | WHY: <what the requirements miss or get wrong> | QUOTE: <quote>
UNSURE: <id> | WHY: <what you cannot tell, and what would settle it> | QUOTE: <quote>

When none are listed under ISSUE REQUIREMENTS, write one of these lines for
each requirement the ISSUE states, naming it in a few words where the id would
go.

Start each UNMET: line with what would fix it:
- [fix-code] — the change does not do it yet: the code or its tests must change.
- [fix-design] — the REQUIREMENTS miss it or get it wrong, or the issue itself is
  wrong: the design must change.

A QUOTE is either the requirement's own words — "<the exact words>", from ISSUE
REQUIREMENTS or the ISSUE — or the code that shows it — <file>:"<its exact
text>". Copy it exactly: it is checked, and one that is not there makes the
answer unusable.


## What you judge against

Five things, shown at the end of this part:

ISSUE — what was asked for, in the requester's own words. This is the standard.
ISSUE REQUIREMENTS — the issue's requirements, each with its id.
REQUIREMENTS — what the design committed to, each with what was done about it.
DIFF — the change as built.
TEST VERDICT — whether the test suite passed.

Judge every requirement in ISSUE REQUIREMENTS: decide whether the DIFF meets it
IN FULL, and name an unmet one by its id and words (<its id>: <its words>). Read the
ISSUE for what a requirement means. When none are listed under ISSUE REQUIREMENTS,
judge every requirement the ISSUE states.
Judge against the issue's own words, not the SPECs: a SPEC that narrowed a
requirement does not make the narrowed version enough. A requirement met only
partly — a subset of the cases, a weaker condition, some of the files — is unmet.

An issue contains more than requirements — context, rationale, links, history.
Those are not requirements. Judge every requirement the issue states, including
what its tests must catch (for example "putting the old code back turns the test
red"). The pipeline does not check those for you. For each one, ask: if the
change were broken, would its tests catch it? If they would not, it is unmet.

Some REQUIREMENTS were not run against the old code: those that need work but
no code, and those design says are already done. Nothing but you checks them.
For one already done, open the file its evidence names and check the claim
against the code. If you cannot
tell whether such a requirement is met, say so rather than guess: the run then
reports it as open, with what would settle it.

A failing test you cannot trace to the DIFF within a few reads: mark the
requirement it bears on UNSURE, naming the test and that you could not tell
whether the change broke it. Do not
work out why a test fails: that is the build's job, and your answer is lost if
your time runs out first.

ISSUE:
[bug] --resume and --from-stage trust and rehydrate every stage that already ran — the live dispatch path replays from the start today

## Decision

**A resume trusts every stage that already ran.** Each stage the interrupted run completed counts as done, and its outputs are put back (rehydrated) exactly as they were when the run stopped. The run picks up at the stage that was interrupted, which runs again from its start. `--from-stage <s>` works the same way: every stage before `<s>` is trusted and rehydrated, and the run starts at `<s>`.

## What is wrong today

- In `main` in `core/pipeline/runner.sh`, the **live** dispatch-unit loop never reads `resume_mode`, `skip_until_stage` or `stage_statuses`. Only the legacy linear loop (#1807) skips completed stages. So `--resume` replays the run from the start.
- `--from-stage` is validated and `pipeline.skip_to_stage` is emitted, but nothing acts on it. The run says it skips ahead and then replays everything.
- Auto-resume reads `$state_dir/pipeline-state.json` before the run switches to its per-run folder `runs/<run_id>/` (ADR-059), so it may never find the interrupted run's state.

## Which loop is live

`core/pipeline/runner.sh` has two stage loops, and only one of them is live:

- **The dispatch-unit loop is live.** That is the block the runner enters when `_run_dispatch_units` is 1. Every shipped template takes it, because `simple.yaml` and `deployed.yaml` both run the cycle `delivery_loop`. That block returns before the second loop is reached.
- **The legacy linear stage loop after it is not.** It is the loop with `_runner_linear_cardinal`, its "Skipping already-complete stage" branch and the stale-artifact warning. It runs only for a flow with no cycle, parallel or map unit: `--template clean`, a flat per-repo overlay, or `ZBUILD_CYCLES_ENABLED=0`. #1807 removes it later.
- **Its resume skipping is not evidence that resume works.** R1–R5 are about the dispatch-unit loop. No requirement may be marked done, and no change made, on the strength of the legacy loop.
- **Tests for R1–R5 must use a cycle.** They run a template whose flow has a cycle, so that the runner takes the dispatch-unit loop. A flat fixture such as `tests/fixtures/templates/runner-state-dir-minimal.yaml` takes the legacy loop, so a test on it passes or fails for the wrong code.

## ADR

- **Amend ADR-006** (resume contract) with the decision above. ADR-006 is in `config/adr-enforcement-baseline.txt`, so the amendment names its enforcing tests inline.
- **Amend ADR-050 §6** to draw the line explicitly. ADR-050 §6 / #2299 says "never skip a stage on the basis of prior output". That rule governs a **new** run reusing an **earlier run's** work, and it stays. Resume continues **the same run** and is governed by ADR-006. A test pins each side.
- Rehydration follows the same path the hydrate stage already uses (ADR-050, `plugins/tool/hydrate`), so "exactly as before" means the same files at the same paths.

## Required behavior

Write each as a test first and watch it fail.

- **R1.** A run is interrupted during stage *k*. Resuming it does not dispatch stages 1…*k−1*, their outputs are present and byte-identical to what they were at the interruption, and stage *k* is dispatched.
- **R2.** Inside a loop (e.g. build → test), a run interrupted mid-round resumes at the interrupted stage of that round. The loop's iteration count and state are restored, not reset.
- **R3.** `--from-stage <s>` dispatches `<s>` first, with every earlier stage's outputs rehydrated. It never emits `pipeline.skip_to_stage` and then runs an earlier stage.
- **R4.** `--from-stage <s>` naming a stage with no prior output to rehydrate refuses with a reason, and does not start.
- **R5.** Every way to resume (`--resume`, auto-resume on restart, and `zbuild pipeline resume --run-id`) finds the interrupted run's state in `runs/<run_id>/` and behaves as R1. Each has its own test.
- **R6.** A run with no prior state behaves exactly as today. This is a guard.
- **R7.** A **new** run of the same issue still never skips a stage because of an earlier run's output (ADR-050 §6). This is a guard.

## Scope

- **Code:** `core/pipeline/runner.sh` (live dispatch loop, startup resume detection), possibly `core/pipeline/cycle-orchestrator.sh` (loop state on resume), `plugins/tool/hydrate/plugin.sh` (reuse, don't duplicate).
- **ADRs:** `docs/adr/ADR-006-resume-contract.md`, `docs/adr/ADR-050-prior-work-reuse-contract.md`.
- **Tests that pin this behaviour:**
  - `tests/integration/pipeline-resume-test.sh`
  - `tests/unit/resume-default-test.sh`
  - `tests/unit/runner-startup-preflight-test.sh`
  - `tests/integration/core-pipeline-cycle-build-test-wiring-test.sh`
  - `tests/integration/prior-work-reuse-integration-test.sh`
  - `tests/unit/prior-work-reuse-contract-test.sh`
